Glue — grammar

guo experiential

Template: Verb + guo (question: Verb + guo + ma?; negative: méi + Verb + guo)

"have done it at least once" — the have-you-tried-it frame

Wǒ qùguo Běijīng liǎng cì.
Wǒ méi jiànguò zhè zhǒng.

Foreigner traps

  • Using le for experience: Wǒ chī le huǒguō answers 'what did you do', not 'have you ever' — the ever-question needs guo.
  • Negating with bù: the negative of verb+guo is méi + verb + guo, never bù.
  • Stacking guo + le (chīguò le) exists but means 'have newly done' — learners overuse it; plain guo covers experience.

guo experiential — full guide — Experiential vs perfective, negation traps.

kuài/yào/jiùyào…le imminent

Template: kuài / yào / jiùyào + Verb/State + le

"about to / going to" — announcements and warnings

Huǒchē kuài kāi le.
Tiān kuài hēi le.

Foreigner traps

  • Dropping the le — kuài dào alone sounds cut off mid-announcement; the le is what makes it a warning.
  • Using textbook jiāngyào in conversation — it reads newsy and stiff; spoken Mandarin says kuài/yào…le.
  • Confusing this yào with 'want': Wǒ yào chī fàn le = 'I'm about to eat', not 'I want to eat' (that's Wǒ yào chī fàn, no le).

Native notes — guo, and the art of almost

chī le vs chīguò — the tell

Wǒ chī le = 'I ate it' (specific occasion, done). Wǒ chīguò = 'I've had it before' (life experience). Mixing these up is the single most recognizable learner tell in this zone. When a friend recommends a restaurant, the native answer to Nǐ chīguò ma? is Chīguò, tǐng hǎochī or Méi chīguò — never Wǒ chī le.

guo vs le — dedicated contrast — Ten side-by-side example sentences.

guo survives questions, dies in negatives

Question: Verb + guo + ma? Negative: méi + Verb + guo — the guo stays but the verb stops taking le. Wǒ méi qùguò is complete; adding le (méi qùguò le) means something different: 'I haven't been there ANYMORE' — a change, usually complaint-flavored.

guo experiential — full guide — Experiential vs perfective, negation traps.

Kuài… le is an announcement voice

You know it from stations and drivers: Kuài dǎ diǎn le! (closing in on closing time), Kuài dào le (almost there — the universal taxi reassurance). The le is what makes it an announcement rather than a bare observation — dropping it sounds cut off, like an English 'we're about to–'.

kuài/yào/jiùyào…le — full guide — Four-form comparison table and the time-word rule.

Nǐ cāi! is a promise, not a question

The story-opener nǐ cāi commits you to a reveal. Native speakers front-load it for suspense exactly like 'guess what' — and exactly like English, it doesn't wait for an actual guess. Respond with shéi a? and let them tell you.
